intro: The Präludium, first of Berg’s Three Pieces for Orchestra, Op. 6, is a four-minute movement that begins with percussion, builds to a climax for full orchestra and ends on a single tam-tam stroke. Robert Craft conducts the Columbia Symphony Orchestra.

sections.label: A′ · Return of earlier phrases
sections.mNote: Scoring thins until only percussion remains.

cues.title: Opening of the Präludium
cues.text: The Prelude begins with tam-tams, drums and cymbals. Timpani add definite pitches, and a flute and two horns, one muted, enter above them. The strings add pizzicato notes and muted chords.
cues.evidence: Berg, Three Pieces for Orchestra, revised full score, Universal Edition, UE 12194 / W.Ph.V. 432, Präludium, bars 1–5. Mark DeVoto discusses the emergence of definite pitches in his analysis, pp. 3–4: https://sites.tufts.edu/markdevoto/files/2015/10/DreiOrch-English.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bars 16–36, Ein wenig bewegter
cues.text: At bar 16 the score is marked Ein wenig bewegter (a little more movement). Woodwind phrases overlap with divided strings, and the same small shapes keep changing their notes and rhythms. The orchestral parts become denser up to the central climax at bar 36.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition revised score, Präludium, bar 16, Ein wenig bewegter, through the climax at bar 36. DeVoto traces the accumulating transformations in bars 16–36, pp. 4–6: https://sites.tufts.edu/markdevoto/files/2015/10/DreiOrch-English.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Close of the Präludium
cues.text: Earlier phrases return in quieter scoring. Berg gradually removes the pitched instruments and reverses the opening accumulation until only percussion is left. A single tam-tam stroke closes the movement.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition revised score, Präludium, bars 42–56, pp. 14–17: the score recalls the tempo of bar 9, then reverses the opening accumulation. Mark DeVoto explains the returning phrases and final tam-tam, p. 6: https://sites.tufts.edu/markdevoto/files/2015/10/DreiOrch-English.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer of Wozzeck, an opera about an exploited soldier, and of a twelve-note concerto that quotes a Bach chorale and is dedicated to the memory of Manon Gropius.

composer.background:
In 1904 Berg’s brother Charly secretly took some of Alban’s songs to Arnold Schoenberg. Their sister Smaragda had spotted an advertisement for lessons in harmony and counterpoint. Alban was nineteen, a bookseller’s son from Vienna, writing songs and working in the civil service. His father had died four years earlier, and there was little money for tuition. Schoenberg accepted him all the same, though he could not pay the fee. Recalling their first meeting in a recording made in 1949, Schoenberg described “a very tall youngster and extremely timid”, whose songs stood stylistically between Hugo Wolf and Brahms.

An inheritance in 1906 allowed Berg to leave the office. When his mother proposed the conservatoire, Schoenberg heard, he wept until she agreed he could stay with his teacher. Lessons lasted until 1910. The Piano Sonata, Op. 1, completed in 1908, shows Schoenberg’s developing variation at work: small phrases change and grow, through whole-tone passages to a final B minor. The String Quartet, Op. 3, shares its themes between two movements; its opening idea returns near the close.
